title: CVSS 4.0 severity
description: CVSS communicates the technical severity of a vulnerability. Asset criticality, exposure, business impact, and response constraints still inform local risk decisions.
example: Two systems with the same CVSS vector may deserve different response priorities.

title: Base metrics
description: Base metrics describe intrinsic exploitability and impacts on the vulnerable and subsequent systems, assuming reasonable worst-case conditions.
example: Record the vector as well as the numeric score so reviewers can assess the assumptions.

title: Attack Vector (AV)
description: AV describes the context from which exploitation is possible: Network, Adjacent, Local, or Physical.
example: An internet-reachable parser can have AV:N even when a deployment restricts reachability.

title: Attack Complexity (AC)
description: AC captures exploit conditions beyond the attacker’s control that require active evasion or circumvention of security-enhancing techniques.
example: Do not use complexity merely to describe how skilled an attacker must be.

title: Attack Requirements (AT)
description: AT describes prerequisite deployment or execution conditions enabling exploitation, separate from attack complexity.
example: A required race condition can affect AT when successful exploitation depends on a specific execution condition.

title: Privileges Required (PR)
description: PR describes privileges an attacker must already possess before exploiting the vulnerability.
example: Credentials acquired as a consequence of the vulnerability are not prerequisites.

title: User Interaction (UI)
description: UI distinguishes no interaction, passive participation, and active participation by a user other than the attacker.
example: Viewing content differs from deliberately importing or enabling a dangerous document feature.

title: Vulnerable-system impacts
description: VC, VI, and VA describe confidentiality, integrity, and availability impacts to the vulnerable system.
example: Read access to protected data affects confidentiality; altering that data affects integrity.

title: Subsequent-system impacts
description: SC, SI, and SA describe confidentiality, integrity, and availability impacts to systems beyond the vulnerable system.
example: A compromised service might expose credentials used to access another system.

title: Threat metrics
description: Threat metrics capture exploit maturity information that may change over time.
example: Update the assessment when exploitation becomes reliably demonstrated or observed.

title: Environmental metrics
description: Environmental metrics adapt the assessment to deployment-specific requirements and modified characteristics.
example: The confidentiality requirement may differ between a public content server and a credentials store.

title: Supplemental metrics
description: Supplemental metrics communicate extra context such as safety and recovery without changing the calculated CVSS score.
example: Automation potential can help responders plan operations without being added to the numeric score.

title: SQL injection
description: Untrusted input changes the meaning of a database command. Parameter binding separates data from command structure.
example: Use parameterized queries; escaping alone is a fragile defense.

title: Cross-site scripting
description: Untrusted content executes as script in a trusted web origin. Output encoding must match the destination context.
example: Render a chat answer as sanitized markdown and reject unsafe link schemes.

title: Broken access control
description: A user reaches data or actions outside their authorized scope. Authorization must be enforced at each protected boundary.
example: A project lookup verifies ownership even if the client already hides other users’ projects.

title: Security misconfiguration
description: Unsafe defaults, excessive privileges, or exposed administration paths create avoidable attack opportunities.
example: An unauthenticated public database listener is a configuration problem even when the database is fully patched.
